Over the weekend, a relatively obscure Instagram account went viral with an AI-generated knockoff of El Empleo, the acclaimed 2008 Argentine animated short that has accumulated millions of views and several top international festival awards over nearly two decades.

The account, Nightframe, has since removed the unauthorized remake after co-creator Patricio Plaza, who directed the short alongside Santiago Bou Grasso, objected to his work being repurposed to promote a paid AI filmmaking service.

The 30-second knockoff reportedly attracted more than five million views in under 24 hours, despite Nightframe having only around 16,000 followers. Neither of the film’s original directors was consulted before its creation or release.

From Plagiarized Short To Paid Subscriptions

The unauthorized remake was obviously problematic, but the commercial connection only became apparent after a closer examination of the Instagram post.

Its caption instructed viewers to “Send AI to find out how I made this film.” Following those instructions triggered an automated private message directing viewers to AI Film School, a service advertising AI filmmaking instruction for $49 per month.

“So these people were not only infringing the film’s copyright, but also using it to make their AI business go viral and generate revenue,” Plaza told us. “I can’t even begin to list all the things that are wrong with this.”

When we reached out, the person behind Nightframe denied profiting from the video or having any financial relationship with AI Film School.

“I’m a student running my Instagram page as a hobby, experimenting with AI filmmaking,” they told us. “I created a 30-second AI interpretation of the original six-minute animation purely for fun, with no intention of exploiting the creator’s work.”

The account operator said the original film had been credited and denied receiving any money from the video or the account.

“I occasionally share AI Film School’s content but have never received any compensation for doing so,” the operator said, adding that the video was removed after Plaza contacted them.

The account did not offer an explanation for why a video supposedly created purely for fun included a prompt that would lead users to an automated promotion for a paid AI filmmaking service.

There’s a bitter irony in the choice of source material for the AI knockoff. El Empleo depicts a world in which human beings are reduced to tools, their labor and bodies exploited for the benefit of others. Nearly two decades later, the film itself has been repurposed without permission to promote technology that promises to automate creative labor, turning years of painstaking artistic work, two years of hand-drawn work on paper in the case of El Empleo, into an advertisement for AI-generated content.

Disney has lined up its next big AI partner, this time teaming with Adobe on a multi-year alliance to bring customized generative AI models into its creative pipelines across its businesses, including tools that will transform hand-drawn sketches into fully rendered concept art.

Under the terms of the agreement, Adobe will be Disney’s official “AI Innovation Partner” and will give the company access to Firefly, Firefly Foundry, Premiere, Photoshop, and dedicated engineering resources. Together, the companies will develop bespoke AI models trained on Disney IP to “generate commercially safe and production-ready outputs.”

According to the release, the work is already underway, with Walt Disney Imagineering using Firefly Foundry to generate 2D concept art from human-made drawings and create IP-based graphics for its parks development. Adobe will also work with Disney’s StudioLAB on experimental production workflows and ESPN Edge on AI-powered sports content.

The Adobe partnership is only the latest in a string of high-profile attempts by Disney to get ahead of the AI curve through corporate partnerships.

A year ago, Disney unveiled its most dramatic overhaul of Disney+ since the streamer’s launch, including a full-on embrace of generative AI tools for users. Then, in December, the company announced a $1 billion investment in OpenAI, a deal that collapsed when Sora was shut down and before any money changed hands.

More recently, Disney hired former Character.AI CEO Karandeep Anand as its first chief technology officer and committed roughly $180 million to recruiting employees from his former company, as it announced another major round of layoffs in a year largely defined by cuts across the company.

While the financial terms of the Adobe deal have not been made public, such a high-profile partnership once again shows where Disney’s priorities lie. Even as it eliminates thousands of jobs, demands further cost reductions, and commits billions to shareholder-benefiting stock buybacks, the company continues pouring resources into AI technologies that could fundamentally change how creative work is produced, and who gets paid to do it.

The executive shakeup following Paramount’s $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery has reached DC Studios, where James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-presidents after four years. Former Marvel executive Jeremy Latcham will take over as president and chief creative officer.

This latest upheaval is particularly surprising given that Gunn and Safran were explicitly included in Skydance’s new leadership team when the merger closed just one month ago. Their departure adds to a broad corporate restructuring that has already seen Warner Bros. film chiefs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy leave the company, with Paramount veterans Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein taking their place.

Gunn and Safran were appointed in October 2022 to oversee DC’s film, television, and animation businesses. Gunn was tasked with creative direction while Safran oversaw business and production, with both reporting directly to then-Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav. In a lengthy Instagram post, Gunn acknowledged the difficulties of balancing filmmaking with the responsibilities that came with co-running a major studio, while crediting Safran with shouldering much of that burden:

I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years.

Gunn also confirmed that he and Safran remain involved with DC creatively, including an additional project he is currently writing. He also expressed relief at the prospect of returning to filmmaking full-time:

I will miss being the co-caretaker of these great characters, but I’m also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking.

Their tenure included an ambitious reboot of DC’s film and television universe, with animation set to play a more interconnected role alongside live-action productions than it had in the past. Gunn’s original vision called for animated projects to share continuity with live-action titles, with actors voicing the same characters they portrayed on screen.

For DC’s animation operations, the leadership change raises fresh questions about the long-term strategy set up by Gunn and Safran. It’s an uncertainty shared across the newly combined Paramount and Warner Bros. businesses, as executives, filmmakers, and employees wait to see how things will shake out.

Warner Bros. Pictures Animation’s The Cat in the Hat opened with an estimated $30.5 million worldwide this weekend, including $20.5 million at home, according to Comscore/Rentrak figures.

The latest Dr. Seuss adaptation, directed by Alessandro Carloni and Erica Rivinoja, finished second at the domestic box office behind the VFX-heavy monster flick Godzilla Minus Zero, which earned $31.61 million domestically and $63 million worldwide.

The Cat in the Hat opened stronger than many industry outlets had forecast, most expecting a debut in the high teens, but well below previous animated Dr. Seuss adaptations. Universal’s The Lorax opened to $70.2 million in 2012, while Illumination’s The Grinch debuted to $67.5 million in 2018.

A more recent opening-weekend comp is Pixar’s Elio, which opened to $20.8 million before reaching $72.9 million domestically. The key difference here is that The Cat in the Hat carries a considerably smaller budget, reportedly under $90 million compared with Elio’s $150 million-plus price tag. The bar, therefore, is far lower for this colorful kids’ book adaptation, which could also leg out the pre-holiday period thanks to strong word-of-mouth. The film boasts an A CinemaScore and an 81% positive rating from PostTrak respondents.

‘Wildwood’ Holds Strong In Third Weekend

Meanwhile, Travis Knight’s Wildwood continues to boast impressive holding power, earning $7.21 million in its third domestic weekend, down just 20% from its $9.02 million sophomore frame. This comes despite distributor Fathom Entertainment dropping 13% of its theaters in week three, from about 3,100 to 2,693 locations.

After 17 days, Wildwood has grossed around $40.05 million domestically, already surpassing the entire North American theatrical runs of Laika’s Missing Link ($16.6 million) and The Boxtrolls ($17.3 million). The film is also tracking ahead of Kubo and the Two Strings ($48 million) at the same point in its release and looks likely to surpass ParaNorman‘s $56 million domestic total before its time in theaters has passed.

Wildwood finished sixth overall in North America, with a $2,680 per-theater average. Its notably small weekend declines suggest strong word of mouth is sustaining the film’s theatrical run, and plenty of runway ahead.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Paradaïz, the filmmaking debut of Sarajevo-born, Winnipeg-based artist Matea Radic, produced by Jelena Popović for the National Film Board of Canada. Animated entirely on an iPad, the film combines hand-drawn imagery, family photographs, and archival television footage. It qualified for Oscar consideration by winning the Golden Dove for short animated film in the international competition at DOK Leipzig.

Returning to Sarajevo for the first time in 25 years, Radic experienced a sudden fear that war might break out again and imagined pulling a hillside over herself like a blanket. That image became the starting point for a surreal exploration of memory, displacement, and belonging. Drawing on childhood recollections of her family’s apartment and an absurdist furniture commercial, she builds a world where familiar surroundings become both hiding places and reminders of what has been lost.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Matea Radic: It was 25 years after having fled Sarajevo that I decided to return for the very first time. As the plane was descending toward the city, I was looking out the window at the rolling hills, and suddenly, a fear came over me. I started to wonder what I would do if the war started again. And in that moment, I imagined myself pulling up the hill as if it were a blanket and hiding underneath it. This image haunted me for some time before I decided to follow myself under that hill and write Paradaïz.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

I learned so much! This was my first film, and I learned something new at every step of the way. One of the biggest lessons was how important it is to have a team to lean on. I was so lucky to have the wonderful people at the NFB supporting me throughout this project. I’m so used to working on my own, but when you spend so much time on a project and become so close to it, having fresh eyes and new perspectives is essential.

I animated the entire film on my iPad, which made for a really streamlined and accessible process. That said, I found myself craving a more analog experience, and I’m excited to explore a more tactile approach in my next project.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

I drew heavily on my own childhood memories to build the world of the film. After immigrating to Canada, I became obsessed with drawing the floor plan of our apartment in Sarajevo. I think it was my way of holding on to home, of making sure I wouldn’t forget it. Creating the backgrounds for this film really gave me the chance to put that memory to the test.

I’ve long been interested in the space where the absurd and reality intersect. Through the combination of archival elements and my own animation style, I aimed to explore and bridge these two worlds. The photographs in the film are old family photos, and the commercial is from the ’90s, for a furniture company called Šipad. As a kid, I was obsessed with this commercial because I always wanted to live on the ceiling, and these people were actually doing it.

Did making the film change how you think about your memories of Sarajevo or your idea of home?

It brought me closer to my identity as a Sarajevan. I find myself increasingly drawn to music, literature, and visual art from the former Yugoslavia, exploring a side of my identity I hadn’t connected with before. I’ve always had this little “what if” in the back of my mind about who I might have been had the war never happened, and it’s been meaningful to explore that part of myself. Growing up in the diaspora, I often felt that I was somehow incomplete, but I’ve come to realize the opposite is true. Home isn’t necessarily a place, but rather a feeling of being grounded in yourself.

Eric San found a guiding principle for his first animated feature while standing in front of a classroom. Before becoming the popular DJ, composer, and visual artist known as Kid Koala, San trained to be an elementary school teacher, making it all the way to a student teaching assignment. During that time, while watching a mentor quiet a room by lowering her voice, he learned something he would eventually bring to Space Cadet: Give the audience time and space to lean in and find focus.

Opening in select U.S. theaters November 13 via indie distributor Viva Kids, the dialogue-free Canadian feature follows Celeste, a young astronaut embarking on her first solo mission, and Robot, the guardian who raised her. Their time apart sends both into unfamiliar and uncomfortable territory, with only their shared memories connecting them across the vast distance.

Adapted from San’s 2011 graphic novel, the film uses tactile CG animation and an original score, with vocal contributions from artists including Karen O, Emilíana Torrini, and Martha Wainwright, to draw its audience into a cozy kind of viewing experience that is sometimes hard to find in an era of high-energy reels and shorts meant to deliver the quickest dopamine hit possible to impressionable viewers.

Produced by Ginette Petit at Outsiders Films, with a screenplay by Mylène Chollet, whom San speaks glowingly of, Space Cadet evolved from live DJing performances that combined music from the book’s companion soundtrack with short animated loops. Production designer Lillian Chan and art director Corinne Merrell helped translate San’s drawings into a three-dimensional world without losing the original’s handmade sensibility.

Since its world premiere in Berlin’s Generation section in 2025, the film has screened at Annecy and Toronto, some of the world’s highest-profile showcases.

Ahead of the film’s domestic release, Cartoon Brew spoke with San about becoming an animation director, finding a shared language with his crew, and giving a robot a human touch through music and movement. We talked for quite a while, so this interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.

Cartoon Brew: When did you realize your graphic novel could become a feature?

Kid Koala: After the graphic novel was published, I did a handful of shows that were live presentations of some of the themes. I would be up there with my piano and turntables. The original graphic novel had a companion CD with some of the pages scored, so in a way it was a template screenplay for a film that wasn’t made.

My plan was just to have the graphic novel, the soundtrack, and the tour, then move on with my life. But Ginette Petit came to one of the shows. Prior to that, she hadn’t been aware of my work or the book.

Lillian Chan, our head of story and production designer, had done a few cycle animations that ran on screens while I played. That was the first time we saw the characters move to the music. I think when Ginette saw and heard what was happening, the light bulb went off. Two weeks later, we got a call from Outsiders Films about optioning it. That was in 2011.

You weren’t originally expecting to direct. How much involvement did you think you would have?

I’m in the music industry, so I didn’t know anything about film budgets or the size of teams. I’d done animated videos with friends and video games that included animation, but I didn’t really know what went into a feature.

When I signed the option, I thought, “Maybe they’ll call me in a few years and ask me to write a couple of musical numbers.” I didn’t even think I was going to direct. I thought it would probably turn into some other thing with a lot of fast talking and fart jokes.

But Ginette was really moved by the graphic novel and the live show. She originally asked whether we could do it in the scratchboard style I’d illustrated the book with. We did some tests, but it was boiling a lot and became fatiguing to animate and watch. We needed a different method to keep the story intact.

She was also the one who said it should be dialogue-free, like the book. I didn’t expect that at all. She really spearheaded keeping that tone intact, then brought on Mylène, who expanded the universe to fill a feature.

How did music inform the screenplay and eventually the score?

One of Mylène’s ideas was to pick a song and put it on loop while writing each chapter. Usually it was a classic American songbook song, like “Moon River” or “They Can’t Take That Away from Me,” these nostalgic tunes already imbued with feeling.

She picked songs to be the heart of each chapter. It wasn’t going to be a music video for that song; it was guiding her writing.

When it came time to score the film, I got to do my own retro-future versions of these songs and invite some of my favorite vocalists to contribute interpretations. The rest of the music was either templated from the original soundtrack that came with the graphic novel or expanded with different instrumentation and orchestrations, whatever served the scene.

The music was definitely my wheelhouse. Directing animation was the new part, and that was a steep learning curve. Once I figured out the language and terminology, it became pretty fluid. They put together a team already interested in making this kind of nuanced film.

What did learning that language involve? Were you initially giving direction in musical terms?

They were all very patient because they realized I didn’t speak animation in the same way. Maybe three weeks into the process, I realized, “Oh, I need to speak in frames.”

At first I was saying, “When he’s walking, I want his shoulder to hit on the snare drums,” or “on the one,” just music talk. They would say, “You want to hold for a comic beat? Sixteen frames?” At first I’d say, “I guess. Let’s see it.” They’d show me, and I started learning.

With scratch DJing, I’m already dealing with tiny slices of sound, a hi-hat from here, all that attention to really short details. I had to transfer that to the visual world. Once that language was clearer in my mind, it was a lot of fun.

Production began during the pandemic. How did you work with the animation team?

All my live touring was canceled because venues weren’t open, so timing-wise it worked okay. During quarantine, we would do notes over Zoom, or I’d do draw-overs on my tablet and sync music to explain the pacing of scenes.

Maybe twice a month, we would go to the studio. Everyone worked from their own computer stations at home, linked to the main server. When we were starting a new group of scenes, I’d go in and help act out moments, answer questions, and get everybody on the vibe.

My job was also to bring snacks. Montreal’s a food town, and I know a lot of chefs from being a DJ.

They put together an amazing squad. The people they approached were interested in something a little more nuanced, a little less squash and stretch, more emotional and tender. I think there were only 16 animators who did the whole film.

The CG has a tactile quality. How did you arrive at that look?

I have to give it up to our design leads. Lillian Chan and I met at the National Film Board. I’d done music for her short film many years ago, and we’ve been friends since. She’s been a mentor and my spiritual guide in animation. When I signed the option, bringing Lillian onto the team was part of my contract.

She’s a hand-drawn animator by trade. Anytime we get together and draw, it could be my character and she’ll do it better. She can draw my robot cuter and better than I can. I deferred to Lillian for the character designs.

For the sets, we enlisted Corinne Merrell, who did the paper sets for The Little Prince and works on my live productions, including The Storyville Mosquito. Those miniature sets use wood and paint, very tactile materials. Her job was to maintain that paper, handmade look in CG.

Both had a clear idea of how to make space in the frame. We wanted this tender, timeless story to work on the big screen without filling it with information. Leave enough room, musically and visually, for people to bring their own hearts and memories.

Did that idea of leaving space also shape how much music you used?

If it ended up in the score or on the screen, it was a choice. Leaving that space was important because I felt it was more resonant.

I studied to be an elementary school teacher before signing my first record contract. Once, the day after Halloween, I had a first-grade class bouncing off the walls. I was trying to raise my voice and turn the lights on and off. My mentor teacher said, “I’ll show you how to do it.” She went to the story mat and spoke quietly. The class settled down. They were telling the louder kids, “Be quiet, I can’t hear her.”

By being quieter, she made them lean in. I took that to heart with this movie. We’re a small crew, but these elements can have power and resonance.

I’m a scratch DJ. I like to be maximal and add too many notes. Even with the music, I was trying to find the restraint so it worked best with the visuals. But I always want something a little off-kilter. You might hear an upright bass in the score, but if you listen closely, every note was scratched on a turntable.

You also used turntables to give Robot something beyond mechanical sound effects. How did that work?

I have two tracks of just turntables under his movements. Some of it is barely audible. The sound design team would have the cogs and regular robot sounds, then I’d put in a tone I was bending by hand on a turntable to match his head moving.

It gave him a humanity or quirkiness that wasn’t purely mechanical. The first time I heard the sound design, he was coming off as very robotic, even though he was cute. I thought, “What can we add?”

It was a stealth little spice layer. Even with headphones, you might not register it the first time, but if we took it out, you would notice. During exaggerated comedic parts, I might bend it wildly, but often it was just part of his voice. Since there were no words, how he moved was going to make it happen.

What did making the film teach you that you could take back to your other work?

As a DJ, you have your finger on the pulse of a room. With this film, it wasn’t done in one take. Animators take a two-second shot, you see it two weeks later, and this mosaic comes together over time.

What I loved was that somebody would spend a week on one scene and imbue it with humanity, feeling, nuance, and their own story that wasn’t in the direction notes.

There’s a scene where Celeste is waiting in a hospital for news from the doctor. The direction was that she was anxious. The animation team added this tiny thing: Her hand is on her knee, and her knee is jumping a bit. It was so subtle I didn’t clock it the first time. Those little things bring you into the moment.

This was originally a story I wrote, inspired by the passing of my grandmother and the arrival of my first daughter. By the time the film was finished, I could feel everybody’s energy, family, and memories in it. Every microscopic choice, from lighting to texture to sound, was made with such care. The crew did such a beautiful job.

Four-time Oscar-nominated French director Sylvain Chomet has responded to questions about the potential use of generative AI in a new ad campaign he helmed for luxury fashion brand Dior, which had been explicitly promoted as hand-drawn in the original materials released with the short, including a behind-the-scenes video.

Speaking exclusively with Variety, Chomet and his producer Aton Soumache unequivocally rejected viral speculation that many of the frames of the short were generated using artificial intelligence. According to Soumache, the ad was created over seven months by a team of 20 artists, six of them animators.

While denying claims of AI use, Soumache did tell Variety: “We used an automated interpolation system for a very small part of the process, but the film itself is traditional 2D animation.”

It’s an interesting distinction that deserves a bit of scrutiny. First, the original ad was presented as hand-drawn by Dior in its exclusive announcement with WWD (Women’s Wear Daily): “The film we’ve created together for Dior is all hand-drawn using techniques that go back to the 1940s,” Dior’s creative director Jonathan Anderson said in the piece. That description, however, leaves out a major detail about the production process, according to the filmmakers’ own explanation.

Automated interpolation is not necessarily the same thing as generative AI, and encompasses a range of different technologies, including but not limited to AI-powered tools capable of synthesizing new frames. Neither filmmaker identified the software used or explained precisely how the process worked.

Soumache characterizes the interpolation as a “very small part of the process,” which also leaves considerable room for interpretation. Is he referencing a small percentage of the finished frames, the number of shots, or maybe a limited portion of the production schedule? Without knowing what he’s referring to, or even which technology was used, it’s impossible to a concrete conclusion regarding the extent of automation in the finished film.

Of the extra fingers, blurry tree stars, morphing dog collar, and uncanny bee tailors that fueled the original speculation, Chomet offered a more conventional explanation: that his team employed established animation techniques in which exaggerated or overlapping shapes convey movement. Unlike the unspecified interpolation system, these techniques have existed for generations in animation production. They’re foundational to the craft of hand-drawn animation. Whether they explain every instance identified by viewers online is another question, and one that cannot be settled by a general explanation of the technique.

None of this proves that generative AI was used. Nor does the employment of artists over a seven-month production necessarily rule it out.

And that’s been the main problem since the beginning of this ordeal. The language from primary sources was explicit in describing the film as hand-drawn. Now, the filmmaker and producer have acknowledged that intermediate frames were generated through interpolation. But they have not provided sufficient evidence to remove doubt about the potential use of AI.

Until they or Dior provide more specific information about their interpolation tools and workflow, their statements have done little to assuage suspicions.

Given Dior’s status in the fashion industry and its emphasis on the short as a celebration of traditional craftsmanship, greater transparency would go a long way toward resolving the questions surrounding its production.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Daffy Season, directed by Hamish Grieve and Todd Wilderman and produced by Susan Slagle Rogers for Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, with animation by DNEG Animation. The CG short draws on the designs and staging of classic Looney Tunes while incorporating painted textures, hand-drawn effects, and an increasingly expansive approach to camera movement and sound found in more modern animation. It qualified for Oscar consideration through a theatrical run.

Daffy is ready for duck season, but Elmer Fudd has found something more compelling than hunting: World Cup soccer. As the other Tunes all fall under the same spell, Daffy’s pathological need for attention sends him into a world the directors envisioned as a cartoon Dario Argento movie. For Grieve and Wilderman, reversing the familiar hunter-and-prey relationship unlocked the comedy. Their Daffy would rather risk being shot than accept being ignored.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Hamish Grieve and Todd Wilderman: First and foremost, we both grew up watching and loving Looney Tunes. Even though we were raised on different sides of the Atlantic, like so many others, we spent Saturday mornings in our PJs eating sugary cereal and enjoying hefty doses of cartoon violence. Maybe this explains our love of horror, and putting Daffy in a cartoon Dario Argento movie was a dream come true.

Added to that, Hamish is a huge soccer/football fan — come on, you Gunners! — and having Yosemite Sam complain about esoteric soccer tactics was a career highlight.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

The original Looney Tunes were operating at such a high level of creative and artistic achievement, and making something that could honor this legacy was incredibly hard. It made us even more in awe of the original artists of Termite Terrace.

The short became a deep dive into the techniques of the original cartoons: honing gags, milking poses, pushing things until they break. And figuring out how to do it all in seven minutes. We both feel that this short was a boot camp for our animated filmmaking.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

Maurice Noble was the GOAT, but we asked ourselves: If he were working now, what would he do to push the medium forward? We wanted to honor his legacy but also use all the techniques that CG allows. And we didn’t want to redesign or reinvent the characters, but find a version of them that worked and felt true to Chuck Jones’s original designs, especially.

We wanted to feel the hand of the artist in every frame, from the painted textures of the sets to the hand-drawn spittle from Daffy’s beak. The short became a journey from what we think of as classic Looney Tunes, then detoured through horror and ended up in a giant modern stadium.

The filmmaking techniques changed to reflect this journey, going from a muted color palette with film grain, mono sound, and proscenium staging with no depth of field to sweeping camera moves and all the bells and whistles that Dolby Atmos could provide.

Daffy is usually desperate to avoid being hunted, but here he’s desperate for Elmer’s attention. What interested you about reversing that relationship?

This was the key that unlocked the short for us. Daffy’s narcissistic tendencies trump his self-preservation instincts, and this became the comedy engine of the short. A duck that would rather be shot than ignored sounds insane, but this is Daffy we’re talking about!

Awards season is in full swing, and Cartoon Brew is excited to invite you to another special For Your Consideration screening in Los Angeles.

On Tuesday, November 10, we’ll be hosting a screening of Netflix’s animated feature Ray Gunn, followed by a Q&A with director Brad Bird and several key members of the film’s creative team.

Set in Metropia, a gigantic city in an alternate future as imagined from 1939, Ray Gunn follows private eye Raymond Gunn, who finds himself drawn into a case involving aliens, murder, and a multimedia star named Venus Nova.

Written and directed by Bird (The Incredibles, Ratatouille, The Iron Giant), the film marks the Oscar-winning filmmaker’s return to feature animation and brings to life a long-gestating passion project inspired by classic detective stories and science fiction.

Laika’s Wildwood is heading into its third weekend in theaters, having already grossed $32.8 million at the domestic box office and looking to maintain the momentum it built in its second week, when it reached the top of the box office on Tuesday.

Travis Knight’s ambitious stop-motion feature will screen in 2,693 theaters this weekend, only an 8% drop from its opening week last month. The film’s distributor, Fathom Entertainment, says it’s targeting around $5 million over the next three days, which would put the film’s domestic total at roughly $38 million after three weekends, with strong holds in its second and third frames.

That’s an encouraging performance for Laika, which always approaches distribution differently than any other studio of its size and influence. Wildwood‘s current total has already nearly doubled the $16.6 million earned domestically by the studio’s last feature, Missing Link (2019). If Wildwood hits its projected $38 million by next week, it will be within striking distance of the lifetime box office of Kubo and the Two Strings ($48 million) and The Boxtrolls ($50.8 million). That said, it still has a way to go before it might catch up to ParaNorman ($56 million) and Coraline ($75.3 million in its original run).

This is where we point out, once again, that Wildwood is rated PG-13, creating a small but noteworthy hurdle its predecessors didn’t have to worry about.

In our recent interview with Fathom CEO Jason Brenek, he explained how Laika’s experiences with traditional Hollywood distribution helped bring the two companies together:

They knew that they had the base of an audience that they were serving. They also felt, after working within the studio system, the traditional Hollywood system, for the entirety of their existence, that they wanted to have a creative hand in how to reach that audience, how to actually bring their content to their biggest fans.

With a reported $100 million production budget, Wildwood is still far from profitability in a conventional Hollywood sense, but its relatively modest weekly declines suggest that strong word-of-mouth is working and that the film is reaching an audience beyond its initial Laika fanbase.

As we’ve pointed out before, Laika also doesn’t depend on initial box-office run revenues the way other studios do. The company is as good as any at long-term exploitation of its catalog, and has the rare luxury of a well-funded owner who values artistic legacy over short-term profitability.

After we published an article earlier this week about a new Dior ad campaign helmed by four-time Oscar-nominated filmmaker Sylvain Chomet, questions were quickly raised about the company’s explicit claims that the short was hand-drawn, with users across all social media platforms posting images that appear to indicate that generative AI was used in the making of the short.

After taking a closer look at those images and rewatching the short more carefully, it does seem likely that the claims hold some water, and that AI was used to create some of the film’s final imagery and animation. We can’t report that as fact and don’t want to make any definitive claims based on speculation, but the evidence is compelling.

Here are some of the more widely circulated examples people say show clear AI artifacts.

We’ve reached out to both Chomet and the Dior PR team, but neither has yet responded to our requests for comment or clarification. If either does, we’ll keep you updated.

Nothing in the original promotional materials or the accompanying behind-the-scenes video mentions the use of AI, and everything released with the campaign has strong, hand-crafted, pro-artist PR spin. If AI was used on the short and not disclosed, the campaign seems purposefully organized to deceive.

Jamie’s Take: I owe our readers an apology. Our original article described the short as hand-drawn in its title. I based that headline on the materials provided and what I saw in the film, which I should have watched more carefully. I’ve since removed that description from the headline and updated the original article.

I should have taken my time and paid better attention to the video. I was too eager to get the article up and start on my next one. The warning signs were there, and I missed them because I didn’t take enough time to watch carefully.

I still think it’s important to give the people involved a chance to explain their involvement in this project and what they knew about its production methods. Especially Chomet, who has decades of outstanding work on his resume. But regardless of what comes out in the coming days and weeks, or if we ever even find out if and how AI was used, I should have done a better job with the original piece.

I’m sorry, and I’ll be more careful going forward.

Pixar will start 2027 off with a major shake-up at the top of its leadership structure, with general manager Jonathan Garson tapped to succeed Jim Morris as president at the studio and veteran producer Jonas Rivera moving into an expanded role as executive vice president of creative.

The appointments will take full effect on January 4, 2027. Pete Docter will continue as chief creative officer, while Morris, who has been studio president since 2014, will become president emeritus as he prepares for eventual retirement.

In his new role, Garson will oversee Pixar’s production and operations, including producers, department heads, and post-production, working alongside Docter. Both Garson and Morris will report to Alan Bergman, chairman of Disney Entertainment, Studios. The new president explained in a release:

I still remember seeing Toy Story for the first time – never imagining I’d one day work at Pixar, let alone step into a leadership role such as this. Every day I walk in the door here, I’m reminded just how special this place is and how lucky I am to be a part of it. Jim has shown me what it looks like to safeguard this culture of quality, innovation, and creative ambition, and I’m extremely grateful to both him and Alan for their trust and support. It’s a humbling opportunity, and I look forward to working with Pete, Jonas, the production leadership team led by Katherine Sarafian and Lindsey Collins, and all of the extraordinary talent here at Pixar as we continue to push boundaries and lead our studio into the future.

Pixar’s incoming president has worked for parent company Disney for more than three decades and joined Pixar in 2010. Before becoming general manager, he helmed the studio’s marketing and franchise team.

“Jim has shown me what it looks like to safeguard this culture of quality, innovation, and creative ambition, and I’m extremely grateful to both him and Alan for their trust and support,” Garson said in the announcement.

Rivera’s appointment comes with a significant shift in responsibilities. When we covered his promotion to executive VP of film production in 2022, his remit was listed as operational oversight of film and streaming production, with Docter handling creative oversight. Now, Rivera will focus full time on the creative side alongside Docter.

Rivera said:

Ever since I walked through these doors as Pixar’s first production intern, this place, its people, and its stories have been my life’s work. I am deeply honored to step into this new role alongside Pete, partnering with him and Jonathan to support our incredible filmmakers and artists. Jim has been an extraordinary mentor and leader, and I intend to build on the lessons I learned from him as we look toward our next chapter.

His responsibilities will now include Pixar’s directors, creative VPs, and development, casting, and content advisement departments. Rivera and Docter will also serve as executive producers on every Pixar film.

Rivera joined Pixar in 1994 as its first production intern. His producing credits include Up, Inside Out, and Toy Story 4, the latter two earning him Oscars. He also executive produced Inside Out 2, the studio’s highest-grossing film ever at the global box office.

As he sheds some of his responsibilities at the studio, Morris will remain executive producer of Incredibles 3. His new role is said to include talent development and mentoring at Pixar and across Walt Disney Studios, along with technology initiatives that support artists and filmmakers.

In a release, the outgoing president reflected on his transformative time at the company:

Leading Pixar has been the privilege of a lifetime, and I’m honored to have been a steward of its legacy alongside extraordinary artists, storytellers, and technologists who keep redefining what animation can do and expanding the art of cinema. After 52 years in the business, and almost 40 at Lucasfilm and Pixar, I’ll be stepping back from the day-to-day, but I’m thrilled to move into handling a number of special projects, working alongside my friends Pete, Jonathan, and Jonas at Pixar, and of course Alan Bergman, who has been such a supporter of Pixar throughout the years.

Looking ahead, I can’t think of anyone better than Jonathan to carry the legacy of this beloved studio forward. He’s a Pixar person through and through, a fierce champion of our films, our people, and our culture. Pixar is in very good hands.

Before joining Pixar in 2005, Morris held senior positions at Industrial Light & Magic and Lucas Digital. His years as Pixar president encompassed both major commercial successes and a difficult period of restructuring as the studio’s parent company reassessed its streaming ambitions and theatrical business.

In May 2024, Pixar cut approximately 175 jobs, or 14% of its workforce, in the largest layoffs in its history. In a staff memo, Morris connected the reductions to Pixar’s retreat from Disney+ series production and renewed focus on features. This year, as Disney embarked on a massive, year-long series of cost-cutting measures, Pixar was hit by a similarly significant round of cuts as it prepared to embrace a “long and lean” production approach, explained to us by a longtime employee as a strategy that will limit future films to 16,500 person-weeks of labor, down from 18,500 to more than 20,000 on previous productions.

January’s upcoming succession plan now places production and operations under Garson while strengthening the creative leadership partnership between Docter and Rivera. Bergman characterized the changes as preparation for Morris’s eventual retirement, although no specific retirement date was announced.

Pixar’s upcoming slate includes the original features Gatto, scheduled for March 5, 2027, and Ghost Market, due March 10, 2028, followed by Incredibles 3 in June 2028.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Busy Bodies, an American production written, directed, and animated by Kate Renshaw-Lewis and produced by Eric Ackerman through Ackzilla Entertainment. The film blends hand-drawn animation with inkjet and screen printing, with each frame printed at approximately 1.5 inches before being enlarged for the screen. It qualified for Oscar consideration by winning the Grand Jury Award for Animated Short at Slamdance.

Inside a domestic factory, tiny workers manufacture disposable objects under the supervision of giant hands. Inspired by Rube Goldberg machines and a “made by hand” sticker on a supermarket wrap, Renshaw-Lewis turns everyday convenience into an elaborate, unsettling production process. The printed sequences progressively deteriorate as they cycle, while a soundtrack built from vintage synthesizers, household objects, and even a pet rabbit’s chewing adds an ominous undertone to the miniature workers’ activities.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Kate Renshaw-Lewis: This was my first film where the choice of medium came first. I had the opportunity to make a film using printed animation, and I wanted to create a narrative that reflected its mechanical, step-by-step process.

The idea for the narrative came to me while I was grabbing lunch during my lunch break, when I noticed a small sticker on my prepackaged tuna wrap that said, “made by hand.” I started wondering: Whose hand? How did they make it? Will I ever know what goes on behind the fluorescently illuminated presentation of the grocery store? I started thinking more and more about the unknown mechanisms and production processes behind everyday, mundane items — things that tend to go unnoticed.

A big inspiration for the film was the salmon cannon tube: a large silicone tube suspended above the water that transports salmon over large dams. It is such a surreal invention that has become part of practical reality. Rube Goldberg machines were another huge inspiration for the film. Their logic felt so important to the film because of its redundancy and delicacy. I think our production systems are absurd when you break them down — very efficient, and very absurd. So much engineering and process goes into delivering something as simple as rubber gloves, or even something as natural as a lemon.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

A small detail that truly saved me hours of work was learning about the contact sheet automation function in Photoshop. I highly recommend looking into it if you’re printing animation or making contact sheets. Big thanks to Sam Gurry and Brian Smee, who shared that knowledge with me.

I also learned that maintaining mystery throughout the narrative feels so incredibly important to me. Busy Bodies follows a strict set of rules, but the film doesn’t explain them. I find it incredibly exciting and fulfilling to watch films that feel like a window into an entire world. I recently watched a retrospective of Jan Švankmajer’s short films that really highlighted this concept for me.

I find it incredibly important to have a very structured mind map and storyboard before beginning production to ground the film, even if the storyboard is only really legible to me. I also really love creating playlists for my films to listen to throughout production.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

I was teaching printed animation classes at the time and had free access to a print studio. Many choices for the film’s visuals and narrative came from the restrictions of the printing process.

The film uses a combination of inkjet printing, using individual color passes, and screen printing. Screen printing requires separate screens burned for each color, which limits the film’s color palette. Because every line, even the still background lines, is printed for every frame, slight variations create a beautiful rhythm, similar to animated boils but with a different tone.

The animation and background style are pretty limited, too, because I knew the final printed frames would be very small and fine detail would be lost. I scaled every frame down to about 1.5 inches so 20 frames could fit on one sheet, then printed them. The paper texture really comes alive because the images are printed so small and then scaled up. The texture in Busy Bodies isn’t noticeable on the printed sheets in person, but it’s a big part of the film’s visual language.

How did you develop the film’s soundtrack, and what role did sound play in shaping its tone?

Most of the sounds in Busy Bodies were recorded at the Vintage Synthesizer Museum in L.A. I went with my two dear friends and incredible musicians, Arius Ziaee and Alex Edgeworth. The three of us spent two straight hours recording a whole library of sounds that I then sampled and built the film’s score from, with help from Arius and Alex.

I also used a keyboard, a clarinet, and a harmonium. I recorded all sounds outside of the synthesizers on my phone in my bedroom during odd hours of the night to avoid street noise. I built the Foley and sound design using recordings of various items, such as vacuums, pillows, water pouring into bowls, sheets of metal, various vintage buttons, and even my pet rabbit chewing hay.

I particularly love the moment when the glove filled with the small workers disappears, and they scatter, running away: All their footsteps are ASMR-style recordings of my fingers tapping on a small piece of wood.

Major sonic inspirations for this film were Raymond Scott, Joe Meek, and Ursula Bogner, who became a key reference point for the film’s sound design. I’m very particular about sound in my films, and I love sound that blends Foley, soundscapes, and music together. It feels incredibly important that the sound adds a subtle, ominous, dark tone to my films. My animation style, and animation in general, can seem quite cute, like a medium intended for children, and I love adding sound that gently nods toward the film’s darker subjects and layers.

Texas’s next attorney general has a far cooler backstory than his job title might suggest.

Democrat Nathan Johnson won Tuesday’s election, along with just about every other Democrat on the ballot across the state, becoming the first Texas AG from his party since 1994. But before entering politics, he composed music for 67 episodes of Funimation’s Dragon Ball Z dub and several of its movies.

If you’re wondering why Dragon Ball Z needed American music in the first place, Funimation believed a more continuous soundtrack would help hold U.S. children’s attention. The company replaced Shunsuke Kikuchi’s original Japanese score with newly commissioned music, eventually bringing in Johnson for its 2005 redub of the opening 67 episodes. In a 2012 interview, Johnson recalled being instructed to provide music throughout, even when he would have preferred. Apparently, saving Earth wasn’t enough. You also had to stop kids from changing the channel.

To celebrate his electoral victory, we spent far too long listening to a YouTube playlist of Johnson’s work today and picked five of our favorites from his work on the franchise.

The selections include music from Fusion Reborn, whose English-language score Johnson created with Dave Moran. Track titles follow the fan uploads below.

5 – “Welcome To Other World”

Dragon Ball Z’s afterlife is equally haunting and charming. Its music box-like chimes and 3/4 time signature help create an ethereal feeling that fits the shocking resutls of yesterday’s elections.


4 – “Goku Powers Up Kaio Ken Attack”

It’s hard not to get hyped up listening to any of Goku’s power-up tracks, and Johnson and his party colleagues must certainly be feeling at their peaks today.


3 – “Vegeta Vs. (Beast) Zarbon”

For those unfamiliar with the scene, negotiations have broken down. Neither party appears interested in mediation. Sounds familiar.

2 – “SSJ3 Goku Vs. Janemba”

Johnson collaborated with musician Dave Moran on Fusion Reborn, combining metal guitar riffs with orchestral scoring.

1 – “Gogeta’s Theme”

Goku and Vegeta put aside their differences, fuse into one person, and get the job done. Wouldn’t it be great if politicians could do the same?

Honorable Mention – “Piccolo’s Sacrifice”

Piccolo is probably my favorite character in all of anime, so he had to make the list somewhere.

Let us know your favorite tracks that came from the pen of Texas’s new AG in the comments below.
